Course Title: Tools for Mathematics and the Sciences: Calculus
Description:
This course will expose students to certain basic tools and calculations in calculus. Some of the material may be familiar to those who studied mathematics in high school. This course is recommended for all students who plan on taking courses in mathematics and physics. Knowledge of the material discussed in this course will be assumed in courses from these disciplines.
In an article titled ‘The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’, physicist Eugene Wigner wrote “... the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences is something bordering on the mysterious and that there is no rational explanation for it”. Mathematics has emerged as the natural language using which the laws governing the working of the universe can be described; it is also a discipline with a rich internal structure explored through powerful frameworks for description and justification. Whether one is studying black holes or neural networks, molecular bonds or climate models, tiling patterns or cryptography, the use of mathematics is unavoidable. A solid foundation of mathematics is therefore an essential part of the skill set required of every student of the natural sciences; a good grasp of basic tools, examples, and calculations is also essential for those planning to study mathematics in greater depth and rigour.
Remarks: This Course do not belong to any particular discipline, because they are preparatory courses. Therefore, we have discussed with the Academic Office that they should be listed under a separate category in the catalogue, and not under PHYS/MATH/any other discipline.

Description:
Strategy is the process of deciding how to best position the organisation in its competitive environment in order to achieve and sustain competitive advantage. The pace of change in the business environment has increased significantly in recent years leading to disruptions in business models, supply chains and organisation structures. Performance, within the conversation of strategic management, deals with superior value creation for stakeholders. The issue is studied by raising two critical managerial questions:
●        How and why do some firms create superior value for stakeholders?
●        How do they sustain such performance?
The above questions are reviewed in the course by invoking various concepts from microeconomic theories and the functional disciplines of management and integrating them into a coherent whole. A systemic approach, involving internal and external environmental analysis, identifying opportunities, formulating strategies at the business unit level and at corporate level are covered in the course.

Information systems (IS) refer to the embedding of work processes, within and across organizations, in information and communication technologies (ICT) such as computers, communications devices and networks that interconnect them. The mediation of work through information systems can save cost and improve quality, potentially granting competitive advantage to organizations that invest in such systems. Data accumulated through the operation of information systems are also further analyzed using statistical algorithms (data analytics) to reveal novel yet reliable patterns that can be exploited to improve the efficiency and quality of work processes.

The word ‘Marketing’ is embedded in conversations of everyday life, and general perception that marketing is all about selling and advertising. However, marketing is a much larger concept that drives an organization with great societal impact. 4P of product, place and distribution, promotion, and price - comprise the original "Marketing Mix." Together with rigorous and complete analysis of the environment, customers, and competitors, they are the key activities of marketing management, and the crucial ones: failure to find the right combination of the "mix" often result in irretrievable product (or service) failure and severe damage to organizational finances and credibility. This course shall follow a blended pedagogy of interactive lectures, case and caselet discussions, and class activities to introduce the fundamental concepts of marketing to the participants.

This course introduces students to A/B testing in modern businesses. This topic has increased considerably in importance over the last decade, as entrepreneurs have learned to think creatively about how to generate data in more rigorous ways and as developments in information technology have facilitated the development of better data gathering. Key to this area is the insight that correlations do not imply causality and, in almost all cases, cannot measure impact. This course helps design and use experiments and natural experiments to measure impact. The class will assume no prior knowledge. However, some knowledge of statistics will be advantageous, and an interest in writing codes in R will be a bonus.
LEARNING OUTCOMES 
At the end of the course, the students would be able to learn: 
1. The difference between correlation and causation. 
2. Link theory with actionable business decision. 
3. Understand how AB tests work. 
4. Understand how analytics can shape business decisions.

Description: If consumers in developed markets had been consuming corn flakes with cold milk for decades, why should a brand like Kellog’s advertise that cornflakes should be taken with hot milk, almost two decades after its entry into India? Why should a brand like Surf (or for that matter most detergent brands) weave a “story” around its brand with a drama-like ad? Why should Indian brands spend so much on cricket or film celebrities”[1]. Consumer behaviour is a fascinating subject. The course is not meant for addressing the above illustrative questions but for making you learn concepts that can come of help in thinking about how to approach such questions. Aren’t we all consumers, whether we snack on a samosa or go to a gym? Consumer behaviour is “the study of consumer’s actions during searching for, purchasing, using, evaluating, and disposing of products and services that they expect will satisfy their needs”[2]. At the end of the course, you should know the consumer decision-making model, with its stages and their respective elements: input (e.g., marketing mix, sociocultural influences), process (e.g., need recognition, information search, evaluation), output (e.g., purchase, use, post-purchase evaluation). Mastery of the subject will give you an edge for pursuing dream jobs in brand management, advertising, and consumer research. Not only that, but you can also pursue higher studies and path-breaking research.

Description:
This course is the first of a two-part sequence aimed at providing a thorough understanding of the concepts and methods of microeconomics. 
In this course, we will study consumer behavior in detail – looking at consumer preferences, budget constraints, and the utility maximization problem in the framework of Marshallian analysis. We will then learn how consumers allocate consumption, get an insight into income and substitution effects, and derive consumer demand functions. We will take a quick look at game theory, which investigates strategic decision-making among a small group of players. We will also briefly touch upon the theory of producer behavior, beginning with a stylized model of the firm, and understanding how economists model production, and how firms minimize their costs. 
Part two of the Microeconomics sequence will cover producer behavior in greater detail, and examine how producers, consumers and the government interact in different settings.

Description:
This course introduces students to mathematical and statistical techniques for conducting empirical analysis in economics. It lays the foundations for the study of techniques to estimate and test hypotheses connected to quantifiable economic relationships. Students will learn to estimate and test basic regression models. The course will also prepare students to interpret estimated regression models and enable them to explore model biases that arise because of data limitations, misspecification, heteroscedasticity, and other factors. This course is a mix of conceptual understanding and practical application. Concepts will be explored through recourse to the textbook, and class notes and discussion. These concepts will then be applied to data sets while using R, the statistical programming language. 
While a deep treatment of the issues surrounding causal analysis is beyond the scope of this course, we will take a close look at the conditions necessary for causal inference while we cover the course material. Through such scrutiny, we will gain insight into when statistical relationships may be considered ‘causal’ and when merely ‘correlational’.
Topics: Data types, simple regression, multiple regression, estimation, inference, asymptotics, qualitative variables, heteroscedasticity, collinearity, diagnostics, hypothesis tests, miscellaneous specification and data issues.

Description: This is a course on the economic history of Modern India, conventionally dated as the period from 1757 to the present. It aims to introduce to the students economic development and policies pursued in India. It attempts to engage students in locating the Indian economy within the world economy and understanding how the relationship has evolved over time. As contesting perspectives exist they will be exposed to them. The course commences with a study of colonial economic policies and the impact they had on India’s economy. In this section students read the work of some major historians. The course then moves on a study of the evolution of India’s economy since 1947, taking the student through the Nehru era, the Indira Gandhi years, the reforms of 1991 and economic performance under the Modi government. In this section the students will read the work of leading Indian economists. The topics covered will include the Colonialisation of India’s economy, the De-industrialisation debate, Land tenure legislation and its enduring consequences, Famines and the Raj, Colonial institutions, the Origins of modern industry, the Nehru era: Planning and its critics, the Green Revolution, initial Liberalisation moves, ‘1991’, the Modi years: initiatives (‘Make in India’, demonetisation) and shocks (Covid 19).

Description: This is a one-term course in certain core areas of macroeconomics that could not be covered in some detail in Macroeconomics I and Macroeconomics II. In seeking to first establish a strong foundation in economic analysis, and in macroeconomic analysis in particular, the preceding two courses in macroeconomics stayed away from controversies in macroeconomic theory between different schools of thought. Further, some important parts of applied macroeconomic theory, like financial markets and financial crises, could not be dealt in detail in the earlier courses. This course will seek to give a more detailed treatment to these foregoing topics. A serious student of economics should not shy away from controversies and unsettled issues in macroeconomics, and should have the confidence to apply his knowledge to popular and important topics like financial markets and financial crises. The focus in this course will be on certain specific topics that any serious student of economics must have knowledge of. Six topics have been chosen for inclusion in this course at an intermediate level: different approaches to macroeconomic theory, theories of business cycles, macroeconomic policy, financial markets, macroeconomic crises and economic growth theory. This course will be pitched at a level that acts as a bridge, for the undergraduate student to continue onto graduate level studies, and also for those who wish to pursue other avenues like business management and employment as economic analysts. Students in this course will be required to do group projects that shall be designed to give a hands-on experience in using software tools for macroeconomic analysis with these objectives in view.

Course Title: Economics and Public Policy: An Introduction
Description:
Given the increasing wealth inequalities, should governments look at Universal Basic Incomes for certain sections of the society? Should AI replace low-cost jobs? Should borders be open or secured? Given rising fuel costs, should governments invest more in alternative fuels or increase subsidies for public transportation? Should government departments and enterprises (railways, airlines, telecom, petroleum) be privatized? These are examples of public policy questions that are inextricably linked to questions in economics. The goal of this introductory course is to prepare students to look at larger public policy questions of this kind and others through the lens of economics, stakeholders, resources use and resource constraints.
This course hopes to cultivate in students an understanding of the underlying issues that influence policy. With political economy becoming the crucial issue of this century, there is a persistent need to develop a deep and specific understanding of the behavior of the markets and the actions of government and the purposes that fashion such arrangements. As the discourse between the economy, society and government becomes clear, so does the use of public policy. It then becomes a visible hand of the government to supplant the invisible hand of the market to achieve desirable societal goals. Working through monetary directions, governmental regulations, legislations, taxation and redistributed transfers, public policy aims to create a level playing field in societies to create growth and development of priority and emerging sectors. In this class, we will develop an in-depth understanding of what public policy is and why we sometimes justify government involvement in solving economic and social problems.
This course aims to provide students with the basic tools to develop an understanding of practical and theoretical issues of the public policy process. Students will get familiar with the nature of public policy and its process, read and discuss theoretical materials explaining the public policy process and describe and analyze practical policy issues policy making - from agenda setting, policy design, policy formulation and adoption, implementation and evaluation. They will also discuss scenarios to simulate efficient and equitable outcomes and also understand the reasons behind policies failing. It will rope in economics concepts of moral hazard, free rider problems, virtue signaling among others.
Remarks: Open to students in years 2, 3, and 4

Description:
This course introduces students to key topics in the field of Development economics and policy, particularly those centered around the colossal challenges facing the global poor.
The first part of the course will introduce students to the fundamental question of why we still see extreme levels of poverty around the world, why some countries are rich while the others are poor. We will review selected classical and contemporary models of development to explore structural and institutional factors that impact the process of development. The second part of the course will dive deep into the concept of poverty at a micro level, i.e., at the level of individuals and households. The course will introduce and encourage students to think about how the poor make decisions, what constraints they face and what difficult trade-offs they make. We will learn about the actions and policies taken by various entities (Governments, international organizations, and NGOs) to improve the lives of the poor. Using modern empirical techniques, we will understand which of these policies have been successful, and which have not. 
At the end of the course, the students will develop a deeper appreciation for the dynamics of the development process and the challenges involved in ending poverty across the world, and have a better understanding of how poverty affects various aspects of human development.

Description:
This course addresses issues related to health care, health policy, using tools from empirical and theoretical economics. We will use the tools of microeconomic theory to study topics such as micro foundations of health (demand for health care), socioeconomic and gender disparities in population health outcomes, health insurance design (moral hazard and adverse selection), determinants of health care spending, technological change in the health care sector, public health insurance policy, and the interaction between economic variables such as consumption and labor supply and health. The primary focus of this course centers on health-related outcomes and healthcare systems in developing countries, with a specific emphasis on India.
Through a combination of lectures, problem sets, response notes to articles and podcasts, exploratory data analysis, and the presentation of research papers, students will learn about research methodology in health economics and applied microeconomics.

Course Title: Biography – a Historical and Literary Exploration
Comment by OAA: Ok. Is this a new course?
Description:
This advanced seminar course (300, 400 and 600) intends to engage with the form of the biography, both as a narrative artefact and as a genre of historical scholarship.
By exploring biographies of ordinary and significant individuals, it will facilitate the discussion of the following questions. What is the relationship between individual lives and their experiences to those of the collectives of which they are a part? How do their lives tell us about the age and the larger events which they might have witnessed, participated or influenced? What light can be thrown on the classic social theory debate on structure and agency through a theoretical study of biography?
A second major concern of the course is the craft of writing biographies. How is the choice of biographical subject made? Is it limited to great man theory or is it possible and desirable to pluralize the subject of biographical writing? How do we write the biographies of different kinds of subjects - pre-modern subjects, modern subjects and living subjects all of which pose different kinds of challenges to a biographer? Should different approaches be adopted by biographers for different subjects?
The course will be reading intensive and will include biographies of a variety of subjects as well as scholarly reflections on the craft of Biography writing. In its first iteration, the course will be team taught with one course coordinator anchoring the course but future iterations of this course may also have a single instructor. The course readings will cover ancient, medieval and modern Indian as well as world history, the themes of race and gender, the fields of science, literature, and social activism, studies of a single person plus of two or more biographical subjects together.

Course Title: How We Became Modern: World History from 1750 to the Present
Description: In this course we will study the history of the last two hundred and fifty years through a focus on key events that have shaped the modern world. This includes the end of European empires in the Americas and their growth in Asia and Africa, the emergence of nationalism, industrialisation and its environmental consequences, the world wars, the Cold War and globalisation. We will look at a wide variety of interesting historical actors from the gaucho cowboys of South America to the final remnants of the samurai in Japan. We will also encounter various important historical figures including Napoleon Bonaparte, Isambard Brunel, Joseph Stalin, Margaret Thatcher and Barack Obama. In studying this course we will gain a foundational understanding of the politics and history of the world in which we live.

Course Title: From Mughaliah Saltanat to Sovereign Republic: India in Transition
Description: This course studies the history of India from the death of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707 to the founding of the Republic of India in 1950. The collapse of the Mughal Empire was followed by a period of competition between various rising powers including the Sikhs, the Marathas, Hyderabad and the Europeans, which eventually resulted in the emergence of the British Raj in India. British colonial rule transformed India. It changed what it meant to be Indian and led to new ways of thinking about nation, religion, and what it meant to be modern. The collapse of British rule in India in 1947 was accompanied by immense violence and lead to the creation of two new countries; India and Pakistan. This course will focus on six key themes; the contest for power among the successors to the Mughal Empire, the rebellion of 1857, the history of the Indian princes, the emergence of Indian nationalism, the two world wars and finally the making of an independent India. The course will prove useful to students interested in Indian history and politics.

This course introduces the rise of civilizations in Bronze Age cultures of Mesopotamia, Egypt, Indus Valley and China. Through the study of material culture, monumental architecture, and written texts, we intend to examine the emergence of complex urban societies, with social hierarchy, political organization and literary traditions. Apart from a comparative analysis of similarities and divergences, this course considers the following themes in each civilization: physical and ecological context, agricultural revolution, the emergence of specialization and professions, the beginnings of commerce and long-distance trade, state formation, urbanization
and town planning, religion, culture, language and literature.

To eat, like breathing, is a biological instinct of our bodies, necessary for daily functioning. Unlike breathing however, the ways in which we eat, the food items we choose or reject, are linked to societal norms and economic capacities, beyond individual agency. This course will read foodways as systems of communications that encode identities in terms of state and household institutions, geographical markers, religious affiliations, labour and class positions, and caste and gender norms. 
This course will move chronologically through the turn to agriculture, ancient states and empires, religious sacrifices and asceticism, medieval mercantilism, industrialisation and circulation of food and labour, and end in the present day post-globalisation world. We will learn to read primary sources ranging from the pots and pans of the ancient world, medicinal texts, religious canonical literature, oral and written recipe collections, and modern day popular culture. Together, we will use these contexts and sources to understand how food functions as a marker of identity.

Course Title: Self, State and Society: Philosophical Perspectives
Description:
There is an intricate dialectical relation between the concepts of self, state and society, and these relations are negotiated in every age, differently. It is important to understand these relations, as they provide us with the rationale for our understanding of ourselves, and our place in the social and political domains. These relations also determine the possibilities and limits of our own agency and actions vis-à-vis others. This course will introduce some of the fundamental philosophical presuppositions that allow this negotiation to take place in the modern age. The course is divided into three modules that discuss the constitution of the self, the state, and the social, in the contemporary modern western age. The objective of this discussion is to not only present a philosophical analysis of these concepts but to also open them up for critique and alternative readings, either from the classical tradition or in some cases contemporary
perspectives. The course is not intended to be comprehensive in its approach to the readings presented, but rather the focus is to have an in-depth engagement with the philosophical
presuppositions of the perspectives presented. Some of the fundamental issues taken up would be: How is the notion of the self, constituted and what relation does it bear to the understanding of the modern age, and the state? What are the fundamental presuppositions that characterise the foundations of the modern state? What are some of the theoretical alternatives to this understanding of the state? What is the role of the social, as presented through the institution of the family, in this matrix? What is the relation that the family bears to the state, and the self?

This course provides an introduction to Vedānta, one of the major schools of Indian philosophy. It explores the key concepts of Vedānta as discussed in the three sources (prasthānatrayī) i.e., Upanishads, Bhagavadgītā and Brahmasūtra. It begins with exploring the fundamental concepts of Brahman, ātman, māyā, jagat and jīvanmukti in these three source texts. Vedānta philosophy employs a number of approaches to unfold the identity between the individual and consciousness (the self). We will discuss some of the important approaches, such as, the cause-effect, the three states, the five sheaths and the seer-seen approach in detail. Through these, we gain a deeper understanding of Vedāntic thought. Moving forward, the course discusses the sub-schools of Vedānta. While the non-dual (advaita) Vedanta of Śankarācārya has become synonymous with the whole Vedānta philosophy, we study it in contrast with two other schools, dual (dvaita) Vedanta of Madhvācārya and qualified non-dual (viśiṣṭādvaita) Vedānta of Rāmānujācārya. The idea is to understand that while relying on the same source text, the variety of interpretation and analysis gives rise to a new philosophy within a system. The course gives an insight into the significance of Vedānta within the larger framework of Indian philosophical thought.

Course Title: Practical Reason and Moral Emotion: Early Modern Moral Philosophy
Description:
The views of Hume and Kant on morality are arguably the two most significant approaches to
moral philosophy during the early modern period. As Thomas Nagel rightly puts it, contemporary moral philosophy “continues to be dominated by the disagreement[s] between [the ethical views of] these two giants” (Nagel, “The Taste of Being Moral”, 2012). It is a well- known fact that Kant initially subscribed to the moral sentimentalist tradition that Hume belonged to, before breaking away as a hardcore moral rationalist. The nature of this decisive break is the starting point between many contrasting perspectives within contemporary meta-ethics and moral psychology –  emotivism/cognitivism, moral sense/intuitionism, Humean motivation/Kantian motivation etc. There is therefore a need to backtrack and read Hume’s and Kant’s original contributions to moral philosophy. Through selected primary source readings, the course aims to provide an overview of the central tenets of Hume’s and Kant’s moral philosophy. The course will begin with a useful background on the broader themes in early modern moral philosophy. Students will be then be introduced to Hume’s psychology of action via readings from the first two books of his Treatise. Then, the focus will shift to the core of Hume’s moral philosophy – his anti-rationalism and sentimentalism – that he develops in the third book of the Treatise and in some sections of his second Enquiry. After discussions on Hume’s moral theory, the course will shift its direction towards the rationalist account of morality that Kant propounded as a reaction to the moral sentimentalist tradition. Students will closely engage with Kant’s Groundwork for a deep understanding of the central themes of Kant’s moral theory - practical reason, categorical imperative, autonomy, duty, good will and dignity. Elements of Kant’s moral psychology such as moral motivation, moral incentive, choice and responsibility will also be explored through readings from his second Critique. The course will conclude by highlighting the significance of Hume’s and Kant’s moral theories to
contemporary moral philosophy.

Course Title: Close Encounters!: Philosophical Approaches to Science Fiction and Fantasy
Description:
 Can science fiction and fantasy suggest questions of a philosophical kind? Do they provoke
philosophical thinking?
 Can they help us imagine our own lived experiences and realities differently?
 Is science fiction and fantasy of any use at all in helping us understand otherwise difficult
philosophical concepts, problems, and theses?
In this course, we will examine an interesting array of philosophical topics seen through equally interesting science fiction and fantasy (SFF) in their different transmedial avatars. Beginning with fiction that challenges our everyday understanding of language and communication, we will
proceed to discuss texts that touch upon our ethical responsibility toward others, on the philosophy of race and gender, as well as on post- and transhumanism. We will learn about the concepts of possible and impossible worlds and see for ourselves whether they apply to imaginary, fictional worlds. We will also experience how SFF narratives confound us with their treatments of time travel. Confronting the (in)famous paradox of fiction, we will conclude this course by reflecting upon our own experiences of believing what we know about SFF.

How do we make sense of global politics in an era where the state appears at once both durable and highly permeable and interconnected, when the increasing power of corporations and media transcend national borders, and when the structures that determine our collective political life appear to be both institutionally obdurate and physically unsustainable? This course builds on POLT 205 Introduction to Global Politics, focusing on contemporary challenges and systemic perspectives that have been developed to help us grasp the structures, agents, and mechanisms of global political order. We begin with an engagement with genealogies of how “the global” emerges as a domain and frame of systemic analysis, as distinct from the idea of the “international”. We move to three major conceptual domains in which global politics is theorised: structures and institutions of global democracy, governance, representation, and participation; changes in the temporalities and frameworks of conflict and its resolution – from new modes of warfare to new regimes of global justice; and the ways in which movements and flows – of people, commodities, capital, knowledge, ideas, identities, and solidarities – shape and restructure global politics. We will grapple with the question of how to identify and theorise changes, as well as to see the durable dynamics underlying changing systems, on a global scale.

Course Title: Comparative Politics I (Formerly: Introduction to Comparative Politics
Description:
This course is designed as an introduction to Comparative Politics, a sub-discipline in the study of politics. Comparative Politics is traditionally defined in two ways. First, in contrast to one’s own, which Political Science students would devote an entire course to. Second, it is defined by the use of the Comparative method, the underlying assumption of which is that all
knowledge is relative. We learn new things with reference to what we already know, and our assessments are usually implicitly or explicitly relative. Comparative Politics as a field trains
us to do this systematically with regard to matters political. everyday ideas, such as the ‘state’ or ‘nation,’ and with the most common arrangements of government, will be this course’s priority. Thus, as an introduction, this course will cover foundational concepts, the organization of government, political systems and central political questions. The idea is that students who are interested in politics and who are interested in informed citizenship, will leave the course with clarity about the words, ideas, arrangements and processes that make up everyday politics—such as different kinds of legislatures or different levels of government or different election procedures. This clarity is the foundation of advanced, complex political analysis
Is this course prerequisites for any fut: Required for Comparative Politics II that is offered for 3rd and 4th year students.

Description: The process of establishing an identity as a modern democratic sovereign state was not easy for India. Especially because this required the diversity and plurality of identities to be anchored to a common universally accepted idea or imagination of the nation. The history of india is replete with civilisational encounters and invasions. However, India distinctively transformed invasions into accommodation, rupture into continuity and division into diversity as argued by Sunil Khilnani. Thus, the success or failure of the state is deeply contingent on understanding its constraints and compulsions. It is deeply connected to the success of democracy in accommodating and nurturing the diversity of identities. Diverse identities often come in conflict with each other unsettling the democratic fabric of the state which significantly relies on the principles of liberty and equality to defend itself. Thus, the course will engage with the idea and imagination of India though contemporary debates and challenges around the working of Indian politics. Some of the debates that the course identifies are: the paradox between democracy and development, frequently raising the question of equality; caste and the question of social justice that brings under review state performance and affirmative action; religious freedom and the communalisation of politics that demands secularism be understood through democracy, equality and liberty; regionalism and secessionism that challenges territorial state sovereignty while accommodating ethnic diversity; and the universal and uniform language of representation that addresses the women’s question, nonetheless failing to accommodate the inter-sectionalities and diverse lived experiences. The course is divided into five broad units: Imagining India: Democracy and Development; Caste, Social Justice and Reservation; Religion and Communalism; Regionalism and Secessionism; and India and the Women’s Question.
Remarks: Course plan is under CC reveiw

Course Title: Debating India: Key Deliberations in the Constituent Assembly of India
Description: The Constitution of India with 395 Articles that are organized into 25 Parts and 12 Schedules was the handiwork of the Constituent Assembly that comprised 389-members, who came from diverse social, economic and political backgrounds.  It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. During its more than seven decades of existence the Constitution of India has so far been amended 105 times. Despite such a large number of amendments the Constitution’s Basic Structure and other essential features, such as Fundamental Rights, remained more or less the same. In a country of vast diversity, divisions around caste, religious and racial identities, and glaring economic inequities, such an endurance of the Constitution is an astounding achievement both of the members, who drafted the Constitution, and the vast Indian populace that took the vision of the former into their stride. But what is overwhelming is the way in which the Constitution came to be formulated in the Constituent Assembly, the arguments and counter-arguments put forward and the justifications made in the making of every Article of the Constitution. This is because prior to 1950 India never had any written Constitution. Of course, during the later phase of its rule in India the British regime had introduced a few administrative related Acts in the written-form. But then these Acts became concerns of the British rulers and the educated elite of the Indian. A vast majority of the Indian population, who were largely illiterates, remained unconcerned with those Acts of the colonial rulers. Besides this, the socio-cultural diversity; divisions around caste, religion, region and language questions, economic inequities and other divergences and differences that we experience in our times were also very much alive and present at the time of the making of the Constitution for the nascent independent India.  Therefore, two most pertinent questions to be asked are: despite all those divergences how did the members in the Constituent Assembly come to agree upon a constitutional framework for the future India; and what were the arguments and justifications made in the Constituent Assembly in the making of certain essential features of the Constitution? A critical exploration of these questions would help the students not only to understand the key debates in the Constituent Assembly, essentially it facilitates a critical thinking, a constitutional perspective and a democratic way of finding solutions to numerous problems that plague our current public life.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: An interest in the Indian Constitution and the Law

Course Title: The ‘Strongman’ and the ‘Fakir’: Understanding the Populist Phenomenon
Description: How do we understand contemporary events such as Brexit, the surge in radical right political parties, left-wing anti-austerity movements, and the rise of ‘strongman’ leaders such as Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Narendra Modi? Connecting these phenomena is the concept of Populism that has emerged as a buzzword in contemporary times and holds a relevance that cuts across geographical boundaries. This course discusses the different theoretical approaches to populism such as the ideational approach, the discursive approach, and the performative approach. The course also offers an empirical and contextualised focus on the varying incarnations of populism and populist leaders in global politics. It pays particular attention to the gendered content of populism as a phenomenon and the field of populism studies. The course also explores different approaches to understanding populism’s relationship with democracy, and traces possible responses to the ‘populist challenge’.

Required for: Elective for Social Studies, Philosophy. Literature and Global Arts Majors, and Minors, and Literature and Arts Joint Majors
Description:
This course explores Place, and its co-relate Space, as inspiration for poesis, conceptual category, and line of inquiry in investigating humans and non-human social relations and lived
experience. How have humans construed Place in their relationship with their environments, and with each other? How have they responded to, interacted with and shaped place in action
and imagination? How does the experience of place shape notions of self and other, and produce forms of social and political action? How do the body and the senses become
incorporated in producing particular experiences of Place? How do we perceive and make sense of built environments, and nature as distinctive categories of place-based experience?
We will follow poets, philosophers, historians, and anthropologists as they engage and respond to place worlds, across time and space. We explore three conceptualizations of Place and Space here, from poetics, phenomenology and Marxist social theory as ways to attend to humans in place and on the move.
Remarks: Course is cross listed with Philosophy, Literature and Global Arts. Crosslisting is pending approval by curriculum committee.

Course Title: Religion and Society in South Asia
Description:
This course is about the study of Religion with a particular focus on South Asian religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zorastrianism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism), as they have been studied anthropologically, historically and politically – as daily beliefs and practices, and in relation to wider South Asian culture, history and politics. This course will provide both a grounded study of religious practices and religions in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sikkim, Sri Lanka as well as a postcolonial critique of the study of religions and nationalism in the South Asian realm.
The course will explore why the transformation of the public sphere in South Asia shows the increasing importance of religious movements, and of the political use of religious symbolism in new communication technologies. One of the most important trends in the present era is the attempt to create a homogenous religious community, not only within the national territorial space, but also in a transnational space. If such attempts offer a sense of identity for communities, it also offers a brutal confrontation with “the Other,” however defined. The violent conflicts between Hindus and Muslims, between “high” castes and Dalits, between Shi’as and Sunnis, between Buddhists and Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims are sad reminders of a growing confrontation which is not only regional, but increasingly global.
This course will therefore combine historical awareness, conceptual acuity, spatial mobility. This will lead us to an analysis of the effects of imperial interactions, state formation and how these provide a crucial perspective for the unravelling of the multiple transformations of religion, religious nationalisms, the global framework of religious fraternities, and what informs the choice of certain identities over others.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: None except an open mind and a curious disposition.

Course Title: The Qualitative Method (Formerly known as Researching the Social, Political and Historical)
Required for: Required course for Social Studies Major / Minor, History Major / Minor, Politics Major / Minor, Politics – History Joint Major. Elective course for Environmental Studies Major/Minor and Economics-Environmental Studies Joint Major.
Description: Historians, sociologists, anthropologists and political scientists are all interested in a shared set of fundamental problems: the functioning, reproduction and transformation of social relations. In the process, they study the structures – economic, political or cultural – which underpin these relations. This course is an introduction to the methods social scientists use to understand the state and society in the past and present – the shared questions the disciplines ask and the often - but not always - divergent methodologies they use to answer them, focusing on qualitative research. Qualitative research in the social sciences is significant for theory building and inductive approaches engendered by empiricism through exploration of the field. Consequently, the course surveys the kinds of research questions commonly posed in these (intersecting) disciplines, and how they have gone about answering questions through the kinds of evidence they draw on and the methods they use to interpret this evidence. Students will acquire familiarity with qualitative methods such as ethnography, case studies, life history method, archival work, content and discourse analyses, examining the strengths and limitations of each of these different kinds of approaches to collecting and analyzing evidence. The course will enable students to develop theoretical and practical skills to interpret and critique research on the social / historical / political, and design a research project with specific and testable research questions, focusing primarily on qualitative research design.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: None, except being prepared to develop research questions, and learn research design process on a topic of own choice, in the final four weeks of the course.

Description:
Why are the young women of some communities of Tamil Nadu, for example, expected to marry their maternal uncle i.e. mama? How and why did the Kulin Brahmins of Bengal justify having numerous wives? Traditionally, amongst the Nair, women were financially independent and inherited their mother’s house. Why did British colonialism change certain laws around marriage and inheritance and how did these transform family structures as well as ideas of gender and community in South Asia? Kinship, or how people are related to each other, has been an important way of learning about them and their culture. The categories some of us might have long considered “natural” such as gendered identities, patriarchal norms, social hierarchies, and even political systems, have revealed, especially when considered in light of other cultural systems, as constructed. So when discussing the Nair kinship system or hijra understandings of identity and community, for example, we will explore the role of religion and colonialism to critique traditionally held Western notions as well as deeply engrained religious beliefs, both centring on the patriarchal family and its associated gender essentialisms. 
A close study of kinship patterns from across the world will throw up historically variable, socially produced, and politically charged issues, which will enable us to critically explore the blinkered beliefs held on race, caste, and gender. After briefly situating the anthropological debates on kinship, gender, relatedness, caste, and community, this course will introduce a range of contemporary ethnographies to discuss recent socio-legal and political developments and how these end up refashioning today’s societal norms.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: None except an open mind and a curious disposition.

Description:
This course examines ‘the urban’ as a field of inquiry and theorization from a relational perspective.
The course discusses key thinkers and debates in urban studies and analyses from the industrial
period, particularly from the mid-19th century, to the contemporary period. The course will enable

interdisciplinary thinking regarding urban phenomena, including urban form, social relations and
theorization. We will discuss key theoretical insights and shifts in understanding urban relations by
situating social contexts historically. The course materials will further disrupt the binary silos of
urban and rural studies by interrogating the co-constitution of the urban and the rural, albeit with an
emphasis on forms of urban life. A field trip will further provide first hand experience of the rural-
urban continuum, and facilitate the theorization of the distinctions therein.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Willingness to engage in fieldwork preparation and undertake fieldtrips as per the course requirements
Remarks:
Note on cross listing: This elective course may be considered for cross listing with Politics,
Economics, History and Environmental Studies. The course examines ‘the urban’ as a field of
inquiry and theorization from a fundamentally relational perspective. It discusses key thinkers and
debates in urban studies and is necessarily interdisciplinary in its orientation, bringing together in
particular work from sociology, anthropology, history, politics, economics, human geography, and
environmental studies. The course will enable interdisciplinarity in thinking through the urban scale
and urban phenomena. It will also disrupt the binary silos of urban and rural studies by interrogating
the co-constitution of the urban and the rural. A field trip will further provide first hand experience
of the rural-urban continuum and distinction.

Course Title: Introduction to Sociological and Anthropological Thought
Description:
This required course introduces students to key moments in the development of sociological and
anthropological thought. Starting with the origins of the two disciplines; the ways in which both
disciplines are from inception implicated in the social, historical, political and economic context
out of which they emerged; we proceed to examine how ideas have emerged over time, through
relentless critical inquiry and engagement with diverse and changing contexts. Each module will
introduce students to a particular moment in the discourse and involve engagement with a
selection of representative texts drawn from key sociological and anthropological thinkers. This
is not an exhaustive course on the history of sociological/anthropological thought, nevertheless
the representative selection of texts is aimed at elucidating key theoretical insights of important


thinkers. Students are expected to undertake immersive reading and critically reflect on the ideas
thus introduced and their relevance (or not) in the contemporary world.
Remarks:
Introduction to Sociological and Anthropological Thought (Required)
Note on cross listing: Sociological and anthropological thought overlaps several social
science disciplines, including political science, history, politics and economics, and
provides the social context for psychology and literature. The key impulses of many
sociological and anthropological thinkers contribute to and are derived from across the
social sciences and humanities and this course enables students to grasp the relational
nature of social theory and phenomena. The course tracks key thinkers and debates from
the inception of sociology and anthropology as formal disciplines to the contemporary
period and enables a grasp of shared social contexts across the disciplines.

Description:
The human “propensity to truck, barter, and exchange” (a la Adam Smith) lies at the heart of all
modern economies. And yet, social scientists have adopted widely diverging theoretical
frameworks to understand how market economies function and evolve. At one end, the dominant
strand of economics today takes rational and instrumental action by individuals as its starting
point when modelling market exchange. By contrast, an equally influential stream of social
thought assumes that economic behaviour is conditioned by the same set of social and political
institutions that also govern other types of non-economic behaviour. In this course, students will
be introduced to the latter set of intellectual traditions in political economy and economic
sociology, wherein “institutions” are treated not merely as constraints upon economic behaviour
but also as constitutive of both the preferences and norms that inform such behaviour.
The course is divided into two modules. The first module (four weeks) revisits the work of some
original thinkers to locate the intellectual origins of this field of study. The second module poses
a series of comparative and historical questions that help illustrate the evolution of the capitalist
world economy from the 18th to the 21st century. Some of the possible themes to be covered in

the second module will include: the great divergence, industrialization and financialization,
inequality and social im/mobility, mass education and the establishment of professions, tax
reforms and welfare states, and new social movements.

What constitutes a social movement? Why and how do social movements emerge? Who joins
social movements and why? What strategies do they use? How do social movements differ?
Which resources are essential for social movements? Why are some successful, and some are
not? These are some of the questions that the course intends to address.
Emphasis will be not only on the processes and career of the movements but also on the
conditions and contexts that give rise to collective mobilization. The students will be encouraged
to ultimately reflect on more general questions about the nature of political power, resources,
conflict, and legitimacy, as well as, the relationship between human agency, social structure, and
historical change.

Course Title: Jaalis: Cutting through from the Past to the Present
Required for: Elective Practicum for the Global Arts Minor and the Lit+Arts Major
Description:
The cut work windows, or “jaalis”, as an aesthetic as well as a practical architectural feature, has been used in multiple cultures through history, typically in hot and arid places. This was most famously used, and most well-crafted (in stone), during the Mughal era. Jaalis have been made in wood, stone, ceramics, and even, (rarely), in metal. As this is a ceramics course, we will touch upon all of them and their histories, but concentrate mostly on the designing and making of terracotta clay jaalis.

In this course you will study the history of jaalis and then go through the process of sketching patterns, drawing inspiration from what we see around the campus, to develop and execute your own modular jaali design. You will learn to convert your designs from 2D to 3D and make a sample jaali window section, and fire it. You will learn the processes that the material requires and learn about utility specific design and execution, giving you an appreciation for craft and craftsmanship.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: willingness to work with their hands and get messy
Remarks: Capped at 15

Description:
Written texts have long informed audio-visual media, whether as the basis of story, research or in more subtle ways. Cinema and photography also have a notable history of inspiring writers, and writers sometimes experiment with weaving visual elements into their writing in a manner where the photographs are not merely illustrations of the text, and the text does not simply caption the pictures. Instead, the reader experiences the integrated, mutually enhancing relationship created between text and image.

We will examine the history of this complicated and fruitful relationship between words and pictures, whether in books, in direct film adaptations or in inventive recreations. We will view different kinds of non-fiction films, from classic documentaries to more poetic and elliptical uses of the cinematic medium. Discussing and analysing these will widen the understanding of how words, both spoken and written, work when forming partnerships with moving images and sound.

Course Objectives / Learning Outcomes: Discussing and analysing these will widen the understanding of how words, both spoken and written, work when forming partnerships with moving images and sound.
Remarks: Capped at 20

Description:
The course will begin with a reading of Mario Puzo's 1969 betseller The Godfather, followed by close viewings of the two films by Francis Ford Coppola based directly on the novel – The Godfather (1972) and The Godfather Part 2 (1974). This will become the platform from which we will explore the relationship between written fictions and cinematic adaptations. Viewing the films, we will analyse the choices made by Coppola and Puzo as scriptwriters. What parts of the story were included and excluded in the first film and why? Which bits were then used as a basis for the second film? Which were the completely new story elements? How did that work? As we do this we will also discuss basic western narrative
structures leading up to Hollywood's all-pervading 'three-act' structure. In the latter part of the trimester we will look at the many different 'avatars' and spinoffs the basic Godfather narrative has taken on since the early 70s, both in the west and here in India.
We will view and discuss segments from commercial Bombay cinema's idea of 'The Don' to the plethora of gangster films from the late 1980s onwards, such as Nayakan, Satya, The Gangs of Wasseypur etc. Towards the end of the course we will become familiar with some
of the critiques of and alternatives to the three-act structure in cinema and in written fiction. The course will be based on intensive participative discussions that will center around how written narrative feeds into cinema and also how cinema and cinematic elements now feed
into creative writing of all kinds.
Course Objectives/Learning Outcomes: To understand better the interaction between written fiction and its screen adaptations. How to start thinking cinematically. Students will also gain a basic understanding of scripting, shot-breakdown, dialogue, art direction, acting, camerawork, sound, music, editing and how these contribute to the finished film. Through a process of comparison and analysis the student will better understand how a particular "base-narrative"; can become the fertile ground from which vastly different versions of itself are
generated.
Remarks: Capped at 15

Required for: Elective Practicum course for the Global Arts Minor
Description:
A practicum course that offers students with creative ideas and projects to be matched to industry mentors and work on their projects through to execution. Creative ideas that can be tested out in the real world, venture ideas that can be incubated and see initial proof-of-concept, research ideas that go from page to stage, productions that can be staged - all of these constitute the world of creative ideas within the ambit of the course. Specific weeks focus on different phases of creative ideation, and examples from different creative domains are used to illustrate and mentor students on project progress.
Students will work on a creative product from idea to execution. Design thinking practices, project management tools and ideation workshops will enable students to work on producing a market-ready product. Emphasis is placed on showcasing the product at relevant public forums and thus act as a bringing together of learnings from several disciplines.
Remarks: Class Attendance is essential as a practicum course

Required for: Elective Practicum in for Global Arts minor
Description:
The different worlds of music - genres, traditions and movements are surveyed with both conceptual overviews and practical guided listening sessions. The course culminates in students working on a music production project - which can be a recital, a composition or even a music podcast - depending on the nature of self-paced exploration that they choose to undertake. 
Through guided listening, small compositional projects, analysis and discovery – we discover the diverse world of music in this practicum. We explore traditions, contexts and usage, while studying similarities and dissimilarities across different musical genres and forms. The course will culminate in a music production project - where the class participates in an audience-facing composition.
Remarks: Class Attendance is essential as a practicum course

Course Title: Arts of the Deccan: The Early Modern Epoch from Vijayanagara to the Marathas
Description:
In understanding the history of Indian arts, knowing the Deccan, its place and role, is crucial. In this course we will travel the triangular realm of “Dachinabades” as named in the first-century Periplus of Erythraean Sea, exploring its contours through the lens of its artistic traditions,literatures and cultures. Since this exploration will become very ambitious if we were to cover all aspects of Dakhina (Prakrit) arts, we narrow it down to the Early Modern Period (fifteenth-century onwards), a momentous time of which we have an immediate cultural memory, making the study of artistic heritages a traceable historicity. We will study the Deccan’s unique art forms and cultural practices through music, dance, literature, architecture, paintings, food and fabric that reflect the multicultural and cosmopolitan socio-political ambience in which rulers such as
Krishnadevaraya, Adil Shah, Raghunatha Nayaka, and  Serfoji each played significant roles.
Through readings, viewings and other detailed digital archival material we will learn to close- watch performative arts of the early modern era as milestones in the cultural history of India. The aim of the course is to enable students identify the distinct features of each of historical period such as the Vijayanagara, Sultanate, Nayaka and Maratha as well as to have a panoptic view of early modern era’s artistic legacies whose essence manifests in diverse cultural encounters. The course will prod us to think of deliberate omissions and censoring when the nation-state regrouped its artistic heritages. Coursework will include readings, class discussions-seminars and presentation style disseminations requiring high level of class participation, interactive assignments and some writing work. While the course does not demand any art practice background, those who are practitioners of any genre will be encouraged.
Course Objectives / Learning Outcomes:
To introduce some artistic traditions across genres from the early modern era and help
students learn/read the movement of art through its socio-political legacy
To work on some aspects of embodiment, wherever possible to add value and inspiration
to the course work
To interweave with the domain of history bringing a multi-perspective approach to
learning the arts, history, and society.

Course Title: Performance Practicum - “This is how we Perform Today”
Description:
The journey of performing traditions (dance, music and theatrical performances) into the 20th century is pregnant with its immediate cultural memory. This course will focus on embodied learnings of some of the traditions that have been altered because of the post-colonial censuring that led to a normative establishment of artistic traditions as “classical” and “folk”. Through the course, students will encounter art practices such as Lavani, Gujjili poetry, Karakattam, Raaja paat or  Stri Paat theatre performance and Reality show performances. Through media- embodiment, we will gain foundational knowledge of these forms even as we draw attention to notions of “purity” and “honour” attached to artistic traditions that affect the way we have inherited them. The course uses corporeality in practice as a tool to encounter the socio-political and economic lives of the artistes who practice these arts.

The course does not require the student to have prior knowledge in any art form, but must be willing to participate in class practicums. Grading will be commensurate with willingness and enthusiasm to experiment and learn, rather than expertise in practice.. The classes will be a mix of embodied learnings (music, dance and theatre forms), video footage viewings and discussions on performative traditions.
Learning Outcome

1.Students will learn a range of performative forms, in practice 

2.Students will learn to pause and analyse the nuances of technique in footwork, movements, dialogue delivery and rhythms in each section

3.They will develop a language of movements and also learn of the history and politics of embodied performances
Remarks: Theatre, Dance Practicum
Capped at 20

Description:
The Introduction to Creative Writing is a twelve-week course designed to give students the opportunity to develop their craft via in-class workshops, readings, discussions and one-on-one tutorials. The in-class discussions will also focus on publishing and the publishing industry. The course will include Zoom sessions with authors and literary agents.
This is an intensive course—it will mimic the frenzied pace of real-life publishing. There will be deadlines, drafts and redrafts. We will learn to read like writers and write like writers under pressure.
Students will turn in one fully realized piece of fiction and a story review for the course. For the story review, students will choose a work of fiction by an author who comes from a background different from theirs (we will discuss in class what this means) on which to write a paper and give a presentation.
Remarks: Capped at 15

Course Title: Make or Break?: The Literary Canon
Out on a Quest: Writing a Research Essay
Required for: Required for Lit Majors 2nd year, then Lit and Arts major and finally Lit minors

Description:
This course aims to expand the study of translation to examine adaptation as integral to it. Some theorists (notably Vinay and Darbelnet: 1958) see adaptation as one translation procedure amongst many others; it is seen as a means of attaining ‘situational equivalence’ to deal with issues of cultural transfer that might affect the receiver’s reception or understanding of the text of departure. Whereas, for others (e.g., Gambier: 1992), all translations inevitably involve adaptation, not least because all acts of translation are, simultaneously, acts of rewriting (Lefevere: 1992). In any case, both poles of opinion, in their own ways, underline the importance of adaptation to translation.
Adaptations of literary works to cinema [sometimes described as translation from literary language to cinematic language (e.g., by Cahir: 2006)], offer a fascinating opportunity to study this enmeshed nature of translation and adaptation, and to enrich our understanding of both these crucial procedures of cultural transfer. 
This course will first employ theoretical perspectives to understand processes of translation and adaptation, and to situate them vis-à-vis each-other. As a practical development of this theoretical work, it will then examine the adaptation/translation of works from three literary genres (viz. novel, play and short story) to cinema; by picking up the nuances of cinematic language (montage, mis en scène, camera-pen, auteur-cinema, among others), it will study the translation of the works from words to moving images and sounds.

The course revisits the idea of humour as an artistic, cultural and humane practice and powerful, potential and often radical form of critique across nations, genres, tongues and political climate. The course intentionally mixes up canonical and comparatively unknown texts so that students are able to respond to them both in terms of their own power, as well as their location in cultures from which they emerged

Learning Outcomes:
1. Understanding with various forms of humour.
2. Understanding humour as a historical praxis.
3. Deep engagement with humour as critique of politics, modernity and society .
4. Interrogating the 20th century from the vantage of laughter, satire and insurgent
critique.
5. A wide engagement with works of culture from a variety of contexts.
6. Engaging with a key question of our time: is humour possible in an age of political
correctness.

Required for: Required course for the Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Description: The course is intended for second year undergraduate students and is meant to be an introduction to the physical and chemical principles that underlie and underpin the biology of organisms. The course will help students understand the molecular logic of life; it will enable them to find answers to questions pertaining to the various aspects of a biological system; these are some samples. How, in biological systems, is energy created or captured, stored, and transmuted, and how is the need for energy sensed? What are the energetic and kinetic bases of a biochemical reaction, which is in turn a unit of a physiological process? How are the various biomolecules synthesized and degraded, and how is the balance between anabolism and catabolism maintained? What are the guiding principles of this homeostasis? How are the various physiological processes orchestrated and synchronized at the level of the system? How does a bodily fluid such as blood act as a buffer, and how is this physiologically important? What are the various classes of biomolecules that make up molecular superstructures, and how do their structures help them perform their function? Instruction in the above will help the student to begin to learn to interpret experimental data, and to better understand biochemical research.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at Different Scales, or General Chemistry (CHEM213), or at the discretion of the instructor.

Description: The course aims to bring together and synthesize the various concepts taught in the Biochemistry and Microbiology courses, to enable a better understanding of these subjects through practical application. The practicals will include instruction in basic laboratory procedures, such as the maintenance and use of a laboratory journal, acquaintance with basic laboratory rules and safety regulations, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the measurement of mass and pH, calculation of solution concentrations as normality, molarity, molality, or as mass/volume, volume/volume etc, the preparation of solutions and buffers, the use of basic laboratory glassware/plasticware and instruments, the extraction and estimation of protein or DNA in solution, the use of the compound- and stereo-microscopes, the gram staining of bacteria, the preparation of bacterial media (Luria Bertani or another), the sterilization of labware and media, the preparation of culture plates, the inoculation and culture of media by various means, and the extraction and analysis of bacterial deoxyribonucleic acid by chromatography. The course may also include exercises in the laboratory using data drawn from the literature.

Required for: Biological Sciences Major and Minor (cross-listed with ENVS)
Description: This course is a primer to plant life, covering what comprises the plant Kingdom, how to identify different plants, and how plants reproduce. The first part of the course will explore the diversity of plants from algae to angiosperms. This will include discussions of plant evolution and phylogeny, how and when the first land plants arrived, how plants are classified, and how to identify broad groups of plants including some common Families of angiosperms. We will also explore morphological, anatomical, physiological and other adaptations of plants that allow them to grow in diverse environmental conditions. The second part of the course will focus on the different reproductive strategies of various groups of plants. Some aspects unique to plant reproduction will be discussed, such as alternation of generations in lower plants, and monoecy, dioecy, pollination strategies, double fertilization and embryogenesis in higher plants.

The course is designed for a college level audience, and is intended as a comprehensive foundation for advanced courses that students may opt for in the future. Course topics will be contemporary, and will focus on conceptual understanding and not encyclopedic detail. The course will involve the study of microbes of the various taxa, viz viruses, protozoans, bacteria, algae, and fungi, their place in the evolutionary order of things, their diversity and distribution, and their relevance in the Anthropocene. The course will use a bacterial-centric approach in its treatment of microbial taxonomy, metabolism, genetics, multiplication, and growth. Industrial, agricultural, environmental, and clinical applications and value will be highlighted wherever relevant using microbial archetypes; this will include certain clinically important pathogens and their control, fermentation as an industrial process, the use of engineered microbes in waste processing and pollution control, and agricultural pests and pest controls. The contribution of microbes to human health (as the microbiome, and as probiotics), and societal and environmental health (as degraders of waste) will be discussed. Students will be taught to isolate bacteria from their surroundings, and to examine, identify, propagate, and preserve them. Emphasis will be placed on bacterial genetics, especially the bacterial extra-chromosomal DNA (the plasmid) and its centricity in recombinant DNA techniques or genetic engineering. The course will enable the student to understand the multitudes of microbes cohabiting with humans, and the nature and degree of interaction between the two. Care will be taken to cross-reference concepts taught in this course with relevant concepts taught in earlier courses.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at different scales, or at the discretion of the instructor

Required for:
This is a required course for a BIOS Major in the FYUP, but only an elective for the BIOS Minor and Concentration. 
Required course for the Environmental Studies Major and the ENVS-ECON Joint Major.
Elective for Environmental Studies minor and concentration.
Description: This course covers the fundamental principles of ecology and ecosystem dynamics, relating these with evolutionary processes and introducing concepts of disturbance and resilience. The focus is on the principles of life, how it functions at the population, community and ecosystem levels, relating these with adaptations to unique environmental conditions. This course will be split into four interrelated modules. The first module, population ecology, will deal with the fundamental concepts of habitat and niche, population dynamics (e.g., population growth and regulation) and population structure (e.g., metapopulations). The second module, community ecology, will focus on species interactions (e.g., interspecific competition, predation and mutualism), the nature of communities (e.g., community structure and function). The third module, ecosystem ecology, will take a in depth look at ecosystem structure and function (e.g., energy flow and nutrient cycling), ecosystem dynamics (e.g., ecological succession) and major concepts related to biogeography (e.g., the theory of island biogeography and the major biogeographical zones of India). The final module, conservation biology, will bring together the previous modules and show how the field of conservation biology has harnessed the principles of ecology to manage biodiversity. The course will focus on the principles of conservation (e.g., the design and management of protected areas), ecological restoration and will conclude with some important case studies, frorm India and across the globe, that showcase various conservation/management strategies.

The course comprises a study of the human defense system against pathogens and disease causing agents. It will start with the genesis of the immune system from the lymphoid cells of bone-marrow tissue, and its maturation. It will go on to the molecular basis for determination of self- and non-self, and how an aberration in this process causes the immune system to go rogue and cause auto-immune disease. The course will center around the humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, of their attendant molecular and cellular events, and how the immune system evolves throughout the lifetime of an individual. It will address different aspects of the immune system such as the genetic control of immunoglobulin gene expression, and antibody production, maturation and diversity, and the roles of the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. The modulation or suppression of the immune system for tissue and organ graft will be discussed, as will be the reciprocal effects of disease and the immune system, allergies and the inflammatory response, and the use of the immune-system as therapy against cancer and other diseases as drugs or vaccines. The course will also include the mechanisms pathogens have evolved to evade the immune system, and the state of our knowledge of these systems. The reconstitution of the human immune system in mice will be discussed at length to further enable the student’s understanding of the same.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: None. Recommended: General Chemistry (CHEM213/BIOS213), General Physics/ Physics for Chemists (CHEM210/BIOS210), and Life at Different Scales

Description: This course introduces algorithmic concepts and hands-on experience in the use of relevant tools/techniques for many key biological sequence analysis problems in Bioinformatics/Computational Biology. We will introduce various algorithms and heuristics for pairwise sequence alignment, multiple sequence alignment, molecular evolution and phylogenetic analysis, genome sequencing and annotation. The students will be introduced to the key algorithms and their applications of key Bioinformatics tools like BLAST and its variants, CLUSTALX, tools like PHYLIP for phylogenetic and evolutionary analysis. This course will be cross listed with Computer Science and assumes a prior background in either “Introductory Biology” or “Discrete Mathematics” and will be open to third and final year students majoring in Biology/Computer Science/Mathematics.
