We will introduce various algorithms and heuristics for pairwise sequence alignment, multiple sequence alignment, molecular evolution and phylogenetic analysis, genome sequencing and annotation. The students will be introduced to the key algorithms and their applications of key Bioinformatics tools like BLAST and its variants, CLUSTALX, tools like PHYLIP for phylogenetic and evolutionary analysis. This course will be cross listed with Computer Science and assumes a prior background in either “Introductory Biology” or “Discrete Mathematics” and will be open to third and final year students majoring in Biology/Computer Science/Mathematics.

Required for: Biological sciences Major and Minor (Cross-listed with CHEM).
Description: The cell is an integrated device made of several thousand types of proteins molecules, each of which is a molecular machine to carry out very precise tasks. The cell lives in a complex environment and must make decisions about input signals including temperature and osmostic pressure, biological signalling molecules from other cells, beneficial nutrients and harmful chemicals. Information about the internal state of the cell, such as the level of metabolites and cell damage is also important. The information processing functions, that is, responding to these signals, is largely carried out by the transcription factors and networks. In this course we will discuss the engineering principles of biological networks and their implications in cellular functioning and diseases.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: At the discretion of the instructor

Description: This course will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles and concepts of chemical bonding (Hybridization, MO theory) structure-property relationship (dipole moment, acidity, basicity) in organic molecules. This course aims to equip students with the problem-solving skills in Organic Chemistry. By successfully completing the course, students will have a fundamental background in Organic Chemistry and reaction mechanism.

This course aims to introduce the students to quantum mechanics and demonstrate how the ideas of quantum mechanics help in understanding chemical phenomena and the layout of the periodic table. The role of quantum mechanics in explaining atomic structure and bonding will be established. This is a novel approach and is different from the historical development of the field.

This course will introduce students to the methods of organic synthesis, common name reactions, and the mechanisms in organic chemistry. The focus of the course will be the organic mechanisms that will guide the students to perform stereo-specific organic synthesis. The major ingredients of the most common organic syntheses will be discussed.

This course will introduce students to the symmetry elements in molecules, concept of point group, character table, use of group theory in conceptualizing symmetry properties, application of group theory in understanding spectroscopy, chemical reactions and bonding phenomenon
This course will introduce students to the various advanced physicochemical experiments such as conductometry, pH metry, surface tension, viscosity, potentiometry and spectroscopy.
This course will introduce students to the various spectroscopic experiments based on absorption, emission and FTIR spectrosocpy
This course aims at introducing concepts of electrochemistry and its application in various basic and industrial processes.

Spectroscopic techniques play a very important role in science and technology. It is important to understand these methods to know their advantages, applicability and limitations. Spectroscopy plays a pivotal role in our understanding of matter, energy and their interaction; in addition, it also plays a very important role in materials characterization. A few non spectroscopic methods will also be discussed in this course. This course will cover the principles and application of the various experimental methods and basic instrumentation. Basic high school mathematics and an introductory course on quantum chemistry are prerequisites.

The course is meant to introduce students to the different types of chirality. Concepts of regioselective, stereoselective, and stereospecific reaction will be discussed. Asymmetric synthesis and the importance of chiral molecules in daily life and industry will also be discussed.

Course Title: Molecular Modelling and Simulations - Biomolecules and Rational Drug Design
Description: This course aims to expose students to various computational methods to study many problems of interest in chemical and biological sciences. Students taking this course will learn the principles of computer simulations,  and applications  proteins . This course will be helpful to students who wish to pursue advanced research in computational chemistry and materials science and those who wish to pursue research careers in the industry.

⮚ This course delves into the role of major food components such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, water, vitamins, and minerals. Students will gain an understanding of the chemical reactions that influence food quality, safety, flavor, texture, and nutritional value.
⮚ The course also covers the chemistry behind food additives, colorants, preservatives, and the interactions between food components and environmental factors. Through lectures, few laboratory exercises, and discussions, students will explore the chemical reactions behind common food phenomena like fermentation, browning, emulsification, and preservation. Practical examples such as the fermentation of dosa batter, the Maillard reaction in browning bread, role of preservatives in extending shelf life will be used to illustrate key concepts.

Required for: Required course for the CS major/ minor.
Description:
The course builds on the first course in programming to serve as a gentle introduction to more
advanced ideas in programming with more advanced data structures. Further, it ties up the
practice of programming with reasoning about program performance and correctness. The
questions that motivate the course include:
(1) What does it mean for a program or an algorithm to run at a particular time or
consume a certain amount of space?
(2) What do data structures have to do with run-time and space? How do we build more
efficient data structures, which can computationally capture a range of objects?
(3) How do we make them more efficient? Or handle complex trade-offs that are involved
in this regard.
(4) How do we use all that we know about programming to build implementable interactive
programs of intermediate scale?

Description:
This course delves into the intricate workings of computer systems, focusing on the 
 interaction between application programs and the underlying system software. Through theoretical 
 exploration and practical exercises, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how 
 programs are executed on a system, the role of operating systems in managing resources, and 
 techniques for efficient program communication and concurrency. Topics include the role of the 
 linker in combining program components, the cooperation between modern operating systems and 
 hardware, and the management of program execution and memory. Students will build a strong 
 foundation in the interaction between programs and hardware, setting the stage for advanced 
 exploration. Students will also learn about the basic I/O services provided by Unix operating 
 systems and how to leverage them to build applications for various purposes, such as web clients 
 and servers. Special attention will be given to techniques for writing concurrent programs, enabling 
 efficient utilisation of multi-core processors and enhancing program performance. By the end of 
 this section, students will possess the skills to develop robust, high-performance applications 
 capable of handling diverse communication scenarios.

Description:
This course is a foundational course designed to provide students with a comprehensive
understanding of machine learning principles and techniques. The course explores the basic
concepts of machine learning, including supervised and unsupervised learning, regression,
classification, and clustering. The course emphasises practical application, with students
given the opportunity to work on real-world datasets to solve complex problems using
machine learning algorithms. They will learn to use popular machine learning libraries and
tools, and will gain experience in data preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and
optimization.

1. Probability and Statistics
2. Design and Analysis of Algorithms

fingerprint recognition, industrial machine vision for manufacturing sectors, medical diagnosis, assessment of crops or weather prediction, object detection or recognition etc. This course introduces
students to the steps of a typical digital image processing pipeline , geometric image transformations, interpolation and enhancement techniques.

SVD). This course offers an introduction to a range of essential mathematical topics centred around linear
algebra of finite dimensional real vector spaces, multivariable calculus, and probability. This course is aimed

Description:
This course will begin by providing an overview of statistical thinking: descriptive statistics,
simulating various standard discrete and continuous distributions in R, sampling distribution and its
connection with the law of large numbers and central limit theorem. Secondly, this course will introduce
statistical inference: sampling and its distribution characteristics, point estimation, and hypothesis testing.
We illustrate this module by solving some inference problems using time series data obtained from different
contexts.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Mathematical Foundations to Data Science I
Remarks: Course open to everyone with fullfilled prerequisities but preference would be given to second year students

Course Title: Digitalization and Society: Understanding Risks, Promoting Justice
Description:
In an era dominated by digital technologies, which have seemingly integrated themselves in every  realm of life, and have been taken up by industry, business, policymakers, civil society alike,  understanding the impacts of digitalization on society is paramount. This course delves into the  complexities of digitalization, exploring both its risks and opportunities while emphasizing the  pursuit of societal justice through informed design and ethical considerations. It encourages  students to go beyond the usual narratives of the benefits of digitalization and ask critical  questions which can help shape it in ways that recenter the emancipation of diverse types of end users. The course draws primarily from academic work in the fields of Science and Technology  Studies (STS), Critical Social Science, Feminist Posthumanities and Media Studies. 
This course offers a unique opportunity to explore cutting-edge issues at the intersection of  technology, society, and ethics using ‘real world’ case studies from India, Europe, the US and  beyond. By gaining insights into the complex societal impacts of digitalization, students will be  equipped to navigate challenges on the topic in both academic and industry settings. Whether  pursuing further research or embarking on a career in technology, this course aims to provide a  solid foundation for understanding and promoting justice in the digital age.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: None, but a basic familiarity with concepts in technology, society, or ethics is beneficial.
Remarks: Course open to everyone but preference would be given to second year students

Course Title: Climate Change: Science, Economics, and Policy
Required for: Required courses for environmental studies Majors/Double Majors.
Description:
This course offers an in-depth exploration of global climate change, examining its scientific, economic, and policy dimensions. We will begin by discussing real-world manifestations of climate change and the fundamental science behind Earth's climate system. This includes understanding weather patterns, energy balance, the role of greenhouse gases, and the carbon cycle, along with future scenarios and tipping points.

Students will engage with the latest scientific reports, such as those from the IPCC, to grasp observed and projected changes in climate. We will critically analyse issues of equity and responsibility in climate change. We will deconstruct the concept of “net-zero” emissions, discussing carbon budgets, sequestration techniques, the outcomes of international climate negotiations, and the geopolitics of climate change.

In addition, the course covers practical aspects like carbon footprinting and the evaluation of real-world commitments to achieving carbon neutrality. We will study the impacts of climate change, including compound events, and explore both mitigation and adaptation strategies. Economic aspects such as carbon markets and various economic models will also be discussed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the approaches to addressing climate change.

An overarching theme running through the course will be the issue of climate (in-)justice, which we will examine from multiple perspectives. The course will culminate in end-term projects, in which groups will synthesize and apply the knowledge gained throughout the course.

This course embodies interwovenness, drawing from different disciplines – physics, chemistry, ecology, economics, behavioural science, and geopolitics. Some modules are scientifically and mathematically heavy, and others are reading heavy. Students taking this course are required to keep an open mind.

Elective for LITT
Description:
Environmental studies encompass not only the science of climate change or environmental harm but also communicating these for various kinds of publics. This course moves away from objective and expert accounts of environmental risk and policy to focus on popular and public-facing forms of environmental communication. 
 
Students will read and analyse genres of Environmental Communication like science and nature writing and the photo essay. This course is writing-intensive and the focus will be producing various kinds of
short written and visual pieces and forms of public outreach around case studies drawn from neighbouring ecosystems. As far as possible we will arrange student interaction with some practitioners of these forms.

Course Title: Environment versus Development: the policy dilemma
Required for: Elective courses for environmental studies Majors/Double Majors.
Description:
The growth versus environment debate has been one of India’s nay the global community’s major policy dilemmas for over a century now, exacerbated in the era of global warming and climate change. Further deepening the dilemma are the processes set off by globalization, privatization and liberalization combined with the role of technology in people’s lives.
Yet, this debate has also spurred a new line of thinking and public policies in recent times.
Growth is an imperative for material needs or poverty alleviation. But ecology, too, needs to be healthy, in the absence of which there’s a heavy price to be paid by the humanity, as witnessed in the unprecedented disasters: landslides, recurring floods and droughts, water scarcity or the devastation caused by extreme weather events and the society’s unpreparedness in such cases.
It’s a quintessential “wicked problem” – to borrow from the term coined first in a 1973 paper by Horst W J Rittel and Melvin M Webber, professors of design and urban planning at the University of California at Berkeley (Dilemmas in a general theory of planning) – that does not allow for the best solution but rather only the acceptable compromises.
Questions abound: Is there such thing called sustainable economic growth, as advocated by the different stakeholders? What’s the history and philosophy of environmentalism and the many different tensions centred around these two ideas? How does public policy factor in both?
This course, drawing from field work and theoretical foundations, would offer students of social and environmental sciences with a keen interest in public policy a thorough review of this classical dilemma and the choices a society has and makes. 
From the earliest debates over the construction of large dams, to industrial development, to the ideas of green economy or degrowth, and the history of India’s environmental legislation, the week-by-week sessions would build on the different thematic aspects of this debate and pose before students the confounding questions integral to understanding a public policy dilemma.
For instance, the social and economic fallout of the land acquisition for development projects by the State using the whip of Eminent Domain: What happens to the people who are displaced by development projects? This itself posits several questions for consideration: Is development possible without any environmental, ecological or social harm? Or is there a need for a paradigm shift to strike a balance between the two processes, as the world runs out of time to deal with and eventually fix the global poly-crisis, a term coined by historian Adam Toonze.
With class-rooms discussions intermittent with lectures, presentations and anecdotal stories from the field, this course will dwell upon the theoretical foundations as well as the real-life situations to explore tensions between the cause of environmental conservation and preservation and an inevitability of development for economic growth.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: The course will be mainly offered to ENVS students of the Third Year and Fourth Year as an Elective , but could also be opened up for economics and social sciences majors

Course Title: Alternative Energy on a Finite planet
Required for: Elective courses for environmental studies Majors/Double Majors.
Description:
Transition to carbon-free electricity is central to addressing climate change. These are generally solar, wind, hydro and nuclear – often termed ‘renewables’, ‘green’ or ‘sustainable’. The use of such terms conceals the substantial limitations and impacts of these alternative sources of energy. Energy extraction by solar panels and wind turbines (i.e. their efficiency) are inexorably limited by fundamental physics. Their power densities are substantially lower than those of fossil fuel power plants, and therefore require correspondingly larger land areas for installation relative to a fossil fuel plant of equivalent output. Unless the installation is on degraded land, they can cause serious disruption to wildlife habitats and agricultural lands. We have already witnessed the deleterious impacts of large hydro projects in parts of the country, and those of nuclear energy in other parts of the world. The raw materials that alternative energy installations are composed of and constructed from – metal ores, plastics, minerals – are in finite supply. Many are concentrated in certain parts of the world (e.g. Lithium in Chile, Nickel in Indonesia), therefore subject to the vicissitudes of geopolitics (and pandemics). Large solar and wind power farms also substantially affect the microclimate of their installation sites causing local warming. It is also unclear how the vast – and exponentially rising – quantities of spent solar panels and wind turbines that will emerge within the decade can be effectively recycled. The intermittency problems of solar and wind power are well known, and therefore the need for battery technology – with its own land, water, material and chemical footprints. What does all this mean for India’s ambitious alternative energy programme of 500 GW of non-fossil energy by 2030? What will it affect carbon emissions, air pollution, wildlife, agriculture, and human settlements? This course will be a joint exploration of many such questions. 

This is a **quantitative course** but pitched at high school level of mathematics. The goal of the course, subject to interest and coding skills, is to divide into teams and create maps of India identifying the regions with greatest potential for alternative energy with least impacts – from interwoven science, socio-economic, and ecological perspectives.

Required for: Elective courses for environmental studies Majors/Double Majors.
Description:
Natural disasters are among the greatest threats for human lives and quality of life. This course introduces students to almost all the natural hazards that can cause disasters, from well-known frequently occurring ones to extremely rare ones. The course discusses the causes and consequences of natural hazards, efforts undertaken to predict them in advance and the complications of such efforts, in a fundamental level. The causes of natural disasters are understood based on the underlying scientific investigations. To predict them, routine measurement networks and scientific modelling are required. Finally, mitigating their effect depends on the support and efforts provided by the policy makers.
Contents:
Lithosphere based: Earthquake, Tsunami, Volcano, Landslide, Sinkhole
Weather based: water and wind both contribute to natural disasters: Cloud burst, Flood, Hailstorm, Snow avalanche, Draught, Cyclone, Tornado, Dust storm, Pollen transport, Lightning, Forest fire
Biological hazard: Pandemics and epidemics 
Space based: Space weather effects, meteor or asteroid impact, proximal supernova or black hole 
Role of climate change and other anthropogenic activities in aggravating the hazards

Required for: Elective courses for environmental studies Majors/Double Majors.
Description:
This interdisciplinary course prepares prospective academics, activists, ethicists, leaders, researchers and policy-makers for environmental justice challenges and opportunities in India and across the world. The initial course module focuses on the theoretical foundations and conceptual contexts of environmental justice. Next, an experiential education module guides learners in developing familiarity with the practice of environmental justice. The concluding module on institutional and societal changes for environmental justice further develops and synthesises the theoretical and practical insights generated earlier in the course.

Environmental justice - a discourse that straddles research, policy, and activism – focuses on the dynamics of justice/injustice in environment-related thinking and action. Concepts closely linked to justice, for example - equity, equality, fairness, responsibility, difference, recognition, liberty, dignity, violence, goodness, rightness, etc. - necessarily get included in any analysis of environmental justice. A crude definitional attempt would be to say that environmental justice is concerned with who wins and who loses in any given environmental context, why and how this happens, why this matters to those involved and to all of us, and what can be done to change things around. Further, good environmental justice theory is attentive to questions of difference and colonialism and the multiple crises of contemporary global capitalism; some political thinkers, for example, explicitly identify the goals of green politics as striking at the very heart of the polluted, materialist, consumerist, unequal, and industrial capitalist society.

Mainstream discourses of climate change, sustainability and sustainable development often obscure the injustice and inequity of specific kinds of human activity relating to the environment. Framing issues in the language of environmental justice therefore allows us to excavate these silences in the mainstream discourses of climate action and sustainability, which in turn makes possible a more informed critique of how power operates in the political and governance systems (in India) that govern the environment. Such an understanding allows for an ethical and truly meaningful environmental practice in fields such as academia, business, journalism, law, media, policy, etc.  
Making the quest for environmental and social justice a central concern requires confronting the fundamental underlying processes (and their associated power structures, social relations, institutional configurations, discourses, and belief systems) that generate environmental and social injustices. A coherent political account of how we could respond to these challenges requires the conceptual arsenal provided by environmental justice theory and practice. Ideas of environmental justice therefore enable “new critical engagements with the relations between economy, environment and society, and illuminate the radical potential of sustainability” (Harvey 1996). Such an approach gives environmental practitioners a suitably nuanced, historical, comparative, and ethical orientation for their specific practice. 
Another question of relevance for this course is: what would distinctly non-Eurocentric environmental justice agendas for India and the global South look like? The analysis here could focus on questions such as: do vulnerable people in India suffer the most from current models of development? If so, why is this and what can be done to correct the situation? How can we balance the tension between economic development and environmental protection in specific Indian geographies? What might be the tensions and polarities between conservationists and resource-dependent communities? What kinds of movements, campaigns, programs and projects are successful in achieving environmental justice in the distinctively Indian contexts of unstable federalism, rampant poverty, violent state action, low literacy, identity and coalition politics, endemic official corruption, poor enforcement machinery, etc.? What can environmental justice practitioners in India learn from the global environmental justice movement and from movements in other places in the global South?  

Summarizing the above discussion, an environmental justice approach as understood in this course, therefore: 
a)        critically, contextually and holistically re-examines the foundations of environmental/sustainability thinking and action from the standpoint of justice, and;
b)        applies the insights gained from such a critical re-examination to ethically devise, implement and evaluate new approaches and solutions to pressing socio-environmental problems.   

The course enables learners to develop an 'environmental justice mindset' and to develop familiarity with some commonly-used approaches, methods, tools and resources to augment the practice of environmental justice in varied sectoral/disciplinary/professional contexts. The course will be built around specific exercises and experiential components focused on professional practice that responds to some key problems of environmental injustice. Workshop-style segments will focus on brainstorming, envisioning, strategising, project design, research methodology, team-work, prototyping, documentation, fund-raising, and communication for professional practice relating to climate change.

In this course, students will develop an understanding of the foundations of calculus. The course will provide a rigorous introduction to limits, continuity, differentiability, and integration, in the context of real-valued functions of a single real variable. Students will also be exposed to some of the applications of this material in the form of a short introduction to the Gamma function, a function with numerous applications in many branches of mathematics including mathematical physics, number theory, and probability. 
After completing this course, students will have the ability to prove many of the fundamental theorems of calculus, thus providing a rigorous justification for results they may have seen previously in other circumstances. The material studied here is a fundamental part of any mathematician’s training: it will be used repeatedly throughout the rest of the mathematics major in a variety of courses.

This is a course in numerical analysis for mathematics students which means that the algorithms are motivated from mathematical theorems and the convergence analysis of these algorithms converts those theorems into quantitative estimates. For example, Taylor’s theorem serves as motivation for many algorithms for solving algebraic as well as differential equations. Broadly, this course will cover floating point arithmetic and errors they produce, numerical linear algebra, root-finding, polynomial interpolation, numerical integration and differentiation, numerical solutions of ordinary differential equations, and optimization. This course will have a computational component which will involve learning a programming language to implement the algorithms of this course.

After this course, you will know a variety of standard numerical algorithms in linear algebra, root-finding, interpolation, integration, ODEs, optimization that are relevant in applications. You will also have learnt how to implement these algorithms on a computer and be wary of errors and artifacts.

This is a first course in Partial Differential Equations for Mathematics students interested in Analysis as well as Applied Mathematics as a discipline. After developing some taxonomy of partial differential equations and mathematical prerequisites, the course will be broadly divided into hyperbolic equations on the one hand and elliptic and parabolic equations on the other. While a broad theory will be developed for first order equations; for second order equations, we will focus on the three prototypes, viz., wave, Laplace and heat equations. An attempt will be made to highlight counterexamples since they drive the theory. Those interested in analysis should get a glimpse of how analysis is the bedrock of all PDEs while those interested in applied math should see how Mathematics can be used to explain physical phenomena.

After completing this course, the students should be equipped with the theoretical tools to analyze first order and second order partial differential equations. They should have a good understanding of first order PDEs and the physical models they represent. They should understand well the three prototype equations – wave, Laplace and heat – that underpin and motivate much of the modern theory of PDEs.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Multivariable Calculus or Analysis 3, Linear Algebra

Description:
Topology is the study of spaces and sets and can be thought of as an extension of geometry. It involves the examination of the local as well as the global structure of a space or set. The foundation of General Topology (or Point-Set Topology) is set theory. There are other areas of topology including Geometric Topology, Algebraic Topology, Differential Topology, Low-Dimensional Topology, and various others. 

This course provides a bridge between the basic knowledge of metric spaces and the more abstract knowledge of algebraic topology. In this course, we see how metric spaces can be generalized to objects called ‘topological spaces’ and the properties of metric spaces can be formulated in a more general way for these spaces. We will cover topological spaces, open and closed sets, interiors and boundaries of sets, continuous functions, homeomorphisms, connectedness, and compactness.
After the completion of this course, a student should be able to:
Define and illustrate the concept of topological spaces and continuous functions,
Define and illustrate the concept of product topology and quotient topology,
Prove a selection of theorems concerning topological spaces, continuous functions, product topologies, and quotient topologies,
Define and illustrate the concepts of the separation axioms and countability axioms,
Define connectedness and compactness, and prove a selection of related theorems.

Groups are the mathematical formalisation of symmetry: in this course, students will study their definition and basic properties. In particular, the important notion of a group action will be introduced. Group theory provides an organizing framework for describing the internal symmetries of mathematical objects across many branches of mathematics, while also serving as a useful language for describing many mathematical invariants.

Probability is the branch of mathematics that deals with the study of randomness. The study of probability provides a foundation to systematically explore processes in the natural and social worlds around us. In this course students will be introduced to the basics of probability theory including the underlying axioms, conditional probability and independence, random variables, and distributions. The course will also cover proofs of some of the classic results in probability theory, the Weak Law of Large Numbers, and the Markov and Chebyshev inequalities. At the end of this course, students will have an appreciation for using mathematical formalism in exploring randomness, and develop a basic set of tools to rigorously model phenomena with underlying uncertainty.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Prior exposure to calculus/ Recommended Prerequisites: Proofs and Ideas and Analysis 1

Course Title: Writing in Mathematics and Quantitative Sciences
Description: Writing and communicating mathematical ideas are becoming more and more important to practitioners of Mathematics and mathematically oriented sciences. While Mathematics is concerned with theorems and proofs, disciplines such as Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science, Economics, and Data Science additionally employ mathematical formalism for modeling and mathematical statistics for data analysis. Writing and communication in these disciplines take the form of research publications as well as writing in public forums in accessible language. This course explores writing and communicating mathematical knowledge in two distinct but related registers: technical and non-technical (specifically, journalistic) writing. The first register discusses how to convey mathematical ideas in the form of proofs, model derivations, and statistical analysis to a technically trained audience, while the second register explores how science journalists disseminate these ideas to a wider readership. In this course, the students will read exemplary pieces of academic and journalistic mathematical writing to derive principles of effective communication and implement the same in their own writing.

Description: Mathematics has been the language to express the laws of physics. Students doing physics must be trained in mathematics. Almost every branch of mathematics has been found useful to physicists. This course builds on the foundations laid in Mathematical Methods I. In these courses, ideas from linear algebra, multivariable calculus, complex numbers, ordinary differential equations, partial differential equations and probability are discussed. It is not the purpose of this course to take the theorem-proof route which is of importance to mathematicians. Rather, it aims to cultivate a sense of thinking that has precision and rigour which are essential to physics, and a bent of mind to understand mathematical texts. Completing the two courses on mathematical methods will further equip students to access mathematical biology, econometrics, econophysics, data science and mathematical modelling.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, the work of Faraday, Oersted and others showed that the forces of electricity and magnetism can be explained by postulating the existence of a ‘field’ that pervades through space. This field concept allows us to formulate a combined theory of electricity and magnetism called electromagnetism. We will discuss the laws of Coulomb and Gauss in electrostatics and Biot-Savart’s law of magnetism. The properties of these fields in a medium allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. On the theoretical side, these concepts lay the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – modern theory of electromagnetism.
Is this course prerequisites for any fut: Classical Physcis Fields II, Fundamental of Theoratical Physics (FTP)

Description: The properties of electric and magnetic fields in material media allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. These have tremendous applications in the form of microwaves and electromagnets, and are useful in explaining various chemical phenomena. On the theoretical side, the work of Faraday, Maxwell and others laid the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – the modern theory of electromagnetism. The behaviour of electromagnetic radiation (light) emerges naturally from this theory, giving us the laws of classical optics. The fundamental incompatibility of electromagnetic theory with Newton’s mechanics was what led Einstein to his special theory of relativity.

Newton’s formulation of dynamics assumes the existence of a frame of reference and time that are absolute. This assumption summarizes our sensory perception of the world. Also, physicists believed that a suitable medium is essential for waves to travel. To accommodate the electromagnetic waves in this scheme, a medium called ether was proposed. Its sole purpose was to support the electromagnetic waves. To prove its existence, Michelson and Morley carried out an ingenious experiment to measure any change in the speed of light if the earth dragged the ether along. The experiment did not confirm any change in speed. Attempts to reconcile this result with the then-existing physics framework were unsatisfactory. Einstein, from a theoretical perspective, announced his reformulation of the basic structure of physics in the year 1905. This course is about telling this story in detail.
Is this course prerequisites for any fut: General relativity  will appear in T3/T6/T9.

Description: Matter is in the realm of our direct experience. Matter exists in different forms. Most common forms are solid, liquid and gas. Other forms of matter could be defined as well. But even among the solids, we encounter variety. Some solids are fragile while others are strong. Many solids expand on heating while some shrink, some liquids flow easily while others are sticky, and so on. Also, matter changes from one state to another on altering external parameters such as the temperature, pressure, electric field, etc. There is an obvious need to go beyond cataloguing these properties. Seeking to understand the basis for this vast variety of properties should be interesting, and could lead to innovations. For instance, the origins for revolution in information technology can be traced back to the availability of semiconductor transistors. This course introduces matter and its forms using the conceptual framework of physics.
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Quantum Physics, Energy and Entropy, Statistical Physics (recommended)

Description: This course discusses some inherent properties of matter such as surface tension, viscosity, fluid dynamics, elasticity, and various elastic constants. It also discusses the variation of these properties with temperature, pressure, and shape.  The basic understanding of these topics is helpful for our day-to-day life as well. The knowledge about the above-mentioned topics can bring openings for research in nonlinear dynamics, soil research, and many interdisciplinary engineering domains, especially if somebody wishes to move into the career path of engineering physics such as civil engineering, fluid engineering, etc. Apart from this, a general knowledge about fluids, beams is helpful in many day to day events of life as well, such as why milk spills easily in a carrying container but not oil. In a nutshell, the students studying this elective course can benefit from having more career paths in the future.

Description: This course delves into the transformative period known as the cognitive revolution,offering students an in-depth exploration of its profound impact on the field ofpsychology. The cognitive revolution marked a paradigm shift, moving away frombehaviorist approaches and emphasizing the importance of internal mental processes.Students will investigate the theoretical frameworks and methodological advancementsthat define cognitive psychology, focusing on understanding the formal nature ofcognition. Throughout the course, we will trace the historical development of cognitivepsychology, highlighting key figures and landmark studies that catalyzed this scientificshift. Emphasis will be placed on how cognitive psychologists approach the study ofmental processes such as perception, memory, language, problem-solving, anddecision-making. Building on foundational knowledge, this course will explore how thecognitive revolution redefined psychological research, moving it towards a moreinterdisciplinary and scientifically rigorous approach. Students will gain insight into thevarious methodologies employed in cognitive psychology, including experimentaldesigns, computational models, and neuroimaging techniques. By engaging deeply withthese concepts, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how cognitivepsychology addresses complex questions about the mind. They will learn to criticallyevaluate research, appreciate the interplay between theory and empirical findings, andrecognize the ongoing challenges in determining the formal nature of cognition. Throughthis comprehensive exploration, students will be equipped with the skills necessary tocontribute to the dynamic and evolving field of cognitive psychology.
Remarks: Required course for students enrolled under FYUP, so concerned third year AND fourth year students (i.e. those opting for FYUP) must register

Course Title: Statistics & Research Methods I (Formerly know as "Statistics for Psychologists")
Description: What factors determine student grades? What is correlation between student attendance and grades? Doesbreakfast improve attention? The answer to these questions is not factual but requires evidence whichinvolves gathering data from a sample and then synthesizing the information using a relevant statistic todraw conclusions. We leverage statistical tools and techniques to gather evidence. This course offers anoverview of the research process, use of scientific methods, research designs and the role of theory inpsychological research. Students will further gain hands-on experience in analyzing real data usingstatistical analysis like measures of central tendency, t-statistics, ANOVAs & correlations.Students will learn between-subjects and within-subjects design, the basics of descriptive statistics,including measures of central tendency, dispersion, surveys, such as probability, scales and their uses,ANOVA. The course exercises will rely on hands-on exercises using statistical packages to explore,visualize and analyze these data. Students will delve into hypothesis testing, probability theory, and theconcept of statistical significance. Further, they will learn about various sampling methods, considerationsof sampling biases, and the complexities of generalizing research findings to broader populations. Astudent emerging from this course will not only be equipped to use these tools and apply them, but alsoevaluate any ‘scientific evidence’ critically and judiciously. The students will learn to report and presentdata in a meaningful way, and learn to transform it into different visualization formats and demonstrate anunderstanding of experimental design. This course provides the foundation for the more advanced Statistics and Research Methods II (PSYC 209).
Remarks: Previously titled Statistics for Psychologists (PSYC211)

Description: This course will introduce students to concepts through readings of original papers of the classic studies in Social Psychology. This will serve three important and interconnected purposes. Firstly, students will learn to revisit the classic studies in depth and breadth. Secondly, the selected pieces of work will introduce students to forms of inquiry used in the psychological sciences to produce new analyses and to advance the discipline. Finally, students will learn to critically appraise the work and findings of social psychological concepts reported in public discourse. The course will bridge the gap between simplified concepts in standard social psychology textbooks and the rigour, complexity and uncertainty of findings in the primary literature, including, among others, journals and theses.
Remarks: Required course for PSYC Major and Minor

Description: Counselling psychology stands out as one of the most popular branches within the field of psychology. This course is designed to introduce students to theories in Counselling. Counselling Psychology offers the ways and means to work with human beings in psychological distress. Thus it is the sub-field that not only offers an application of various understandings of the mind, but also an important purpose to the vast knowledge that the discipline generates. The history of counselling is rich and dynamic. It has been influenced by social, political and intellectual movements at various times. This course aims to familiarise the students with this complex past and present of counselling through some of the major theoretical streams that developed within Psychology.Through thorough exploration and critical analysis of various counselling theories, students will delve into the core principles, concepts, and methodologies integral to the counselling process. Engaging with case studies and role-playing scenarios, students will have the opportunity to contextualise theoretical constructs within real-life counselling contexts. By navigating the complexities of counselling theories, students will gain a deeper understanding of the nuanced approaches employed in the therapeutic encounter.
Remarks: Required course under FYUP, but third year students can take it as an elective

Description: This course offers an introduction to the field of industrial and organizational (I/O) psychology, which focuses on scientifically studying behavior within organizational contexts, and applying psychological principles to comprehend and shape work behavior. The course should help students appreciate the human aspects of organisations at individual, interpersonal and group levels. Topics in this course encompass exploring the intricacies of employee satisfaction and workplace motivation, analyzing how various leadership styles influence employee performance and organizational outcomes, and locating sites of intervention for changes. The primary objective of the course is to foster a critical examination of the intricate fabric of workplace dynamics. This includes scrutinizing prevalent workplace practices,  exploring decision-making processes, and examining the criteria used to measure both success and failure within organizational contexts. Through this course, students will be exposed to the multifaceted nature of organizational behavior and the complex interplay between individuals, structures, and culture within the workplace.
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30

Description: There has been a radical shift in understanding of health and wellbeing. The traditional biomedical approach is giving way to a multi-faceted biopsychosocial approach. Similarly, the processes underlying stress, motivation, wellbeing and team performance in sports demand a greater understanding of the athletes as social beings. Psychology has an indispensable place in the scientific knowledge of health and sports. However, the narrow and individualistic theorisation of different micro and macro-level factors remains a critical challenge to overcome. This course seeks to enable the students to navigate these challenges by focusing on the vibrant  psychological processes underlying the fields of health and sports. Taking a lens of groups and identities, we will examine the ‘group’ in the individual that makes these phenomena possible and, at the same time, offers tools for effecting a change. In this course, we shall pursue the questions emerging from the field of health and sports, ground them in scientific knowledge and interrogate them through hands-on exercises.
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30

Course Title: Motherhood Family and Childcare in India
Description: The aim of this course is to interrogate the sociocultural constitution of motherhood as a psychological experience. Challenging the Eurocentric depiction of the mother-infant dyad reproduced in psychology literature, this course approaches a sensemaking process through the intersectionality of cultural psychology, feminist intersectionality, and critical developmental psychology perspectives. Through the course, students will examine motherhood as a social institution and study the nurturing bonds women have with children and others. In so doing, students will focus on analyzing the stereotypical representations of the mothers as “monstrous” and “consecrated”. Subsequently, students will have the opportunity to examine the developmental experiences of women such as pregnancy, childbirth, and caregiving rooted in the family and communal life in India. Students will have the opportunity to understand how family life, cultural practices, technologies, and structural inequities structure multiple trajectories for motherhood and their childcare decisions.  Lastly, taking Burman’s “Child as Method” as an analytic and pedagogical device, students will unpack various contemporary and historical discourses on childhood and parenting shapes and regulates motherhood as a site for “oppression” and “resistance”. We will explore how everyday acts of mothering are performed as resistance to prevailing sociocultural norms.
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30

Description: This course offers an introduction to the fundamental concepts in the psychology oflanguage, exploring the nature of Natural Language and how it is structured andprocessed by the human brain. Students will delve into key topics such as syntax, orsentence structure, and phonology, the sound structure of language. The course alsoexamines the cognitive processes underlying language comprehension and production,and how natural language is represented and processed in the brain. The course willintroduce to formal theories of Language, focusing on Syntax, Phonology andPhonetics, and subsequently guide them through psycholinguistic theories of linguisticprocessing in the brain. Besides being introduced to the theoretical and experimentalconcepts foundational to the field, the students are also exposed to the history of thedevelopment of psycholinguistic thought, and the various frameworks of psychology thatare relevant to understanding Natural Languages. Through a combination of lectures,discussions, and hands-on laboratory activities, students will gain a deeperunderstanding of the complex relationship between language and the mind.
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30

Description: This course will introduce psychoanalysis, focusing on the groundbreaking work of Sigmund Freud that transformed our understanding of mental life in the late 19th century. Although psychoanalysis is often associated with sex, it actually encompasses a broader exploration of societal pressures and the ideologies surrounding sex and sexuality. Freud challenged prevailing psychiatric and psychological models by introducing the concept of the unconscious. Psychoanalysis provides a unique framework to delve into the internal divisions of human subjectivity, particularly through the study of the unconscious in clinical settings. Moreover, it offers valuable insights into the influence of culture and social forces on the construction of individual difference. The course will examine the dynamic interplay between individuals and society, the intersection of clinical practice and cultural context, and the complexities of sexuality and sexual differences. Students will have the opportunity to analyze and critique Freud's theories and methods, encouraging a critical examination of his work while also exploring how contemporary psychoanalysts continue to build upon and refine his ideas.
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30. Open to fourth year and third year students. Fourth year students are given first preference.

Description: Psychology of Disaster Response and Humanitarianism is an interdisciplinary course drawing on thefields of disaster studies, humanitarian aid policy, and psychology. This course will introduce students tothe field of International Disaster Psychology in relation to Humanitarian politics and the intertwinedimpacts that these have on individuals and communities affected by disasters. Through the course, weshall evaluate the defining concepts of disaster, risk, resilience, and humanitarianism, the narratives thatsustain these concepts and which in turn shape policy decisions. From the panoramic view of thepolitical landscape of international agencies like the UN, we shall learn to think with a socialpsychological lens of community and group responses in emergencies and disaster scenarios, bringingthis together in a focused look at particular psychological interventions through different case-studies
Remarks: All PSYC electives capped at 30. Open to fourth year and third year students. Fourth year students are given first preference.
